full_text:
Once upon a time, a poor woodcutter and his wife lived in a humble thatched hut in the heart of a great, shadowy forest. They had seven sons, born in rapid succession: the eldest was ten years old and the youngest was only seven. The youngest boy was remarkably small; when he was born, he was scarcely larger than a man's thumb, wherefore he was named Little Thumbling, or Hop-o'-My-Thumb.

Though he was the smallest and spoke very little, Thumbling was the sharpest and most observant child in the province. While his elder brothers babbled, he listened carefully, storing every word in his quick mind. His parents, however, foolishly mistook his silence for dullness and often laid upon him the blame for every misfortune.

A terrible famine swept over the land. Grain prices rose so high that the poor woodcutter could no longer earn enough to buy a crust of bread for his starving boys. One evening, sitting by the dying embers while the children were asleep in their trundle beds, the woodcutter wept: 'Wife, my heart breaks to see our boys waste away before our eyes. Tomorrow morning, we must lead them into the deepest thicket of the forest to gather faggots, and while they are busy binding sticks, we will slip away and leave them. It is better that they be found by some rich hunter than that we watch them starve in our arms.'

The mother wept bitterly, but extreme misery overcame her reluctance.

Hop-o'-My-Thumb, who was lying awake under his father's stool, heard every word. Instead of crying, he crept out of the hut at dawn, ran to the bed of a nearby stream, and filled his pockets with smooth, white flint pebbles.

After breakfast, the parents led the seven boys into the densest, darkest part of the wilderness. As they walked, Thumbling dropped the white pebbles one by one along the trail. When the woodcutter began chopping trees and the brothers were gathering brushwood, the parents stole away through a ravine.

Finding themselves alone in the gathering gloom, the six elder brothers wept aloud in terror. But Thumbling laughed: 'Fear not, brothers! Father and mother have left us, but follow me, and I will lead you safely home.' Guided by the white pebbles gleaming in the moonlight, Thumbling led his brothers straight back to their cottage.

Listening at the door, they heard their mother weeping: for that afternoon, the lord of the manor had paid the woodcutter ten silver crowns for old debts, and the mother had purchased a great pot of beef, lamenting that her boys were not there to eat it. Thumbling pushed open the door and shouted cheerfully: 'Here we are, mother!' Overjoyed, the parents fed them a bountiful supper.

When the silver was spent, hunger returned, and the parents resolved to abandon the boys again, leading them even deeper into the woods. Hop-o'-My-Thumb intended to gather more pebbles, but his mother had locked the cottage door. Instead, he crumbled his morning crust of bread in his pocket, dropping crumbs along the trail as they walked.

When the parents deserted them, Thumbling sought his breadcrumbs, but in vain: a flock of woodland sparrows and thrushes had pecked up every single crumb! The seven boys were hopelessly lost in the black forest, surrounded by howling wolves.

Climbing to the top of a tall pine, Thumbling spotted a flicker of candlelight beyond the forest canopy. Gathering his brothers, he led them toward the light until they arrived at a massive stone mansion with iron bars on the windows.

A kind-hearted woman answered their knock. 'Alas, poor children!' she cried. 'Do you not know where you are? This is the castle of a monstrous ogre who feasts upon the flesh of little children!'

'Madam,' Thumbling pleaded with tears, 'if you do not hide us, the wolves will devour us tonight. We would rather be eaten by the master of the house if it must be, but perhaps your compassion may soften his heart.'

Moved to pity, the ogress hid the boys under a bed. Soon, a thunderous stamping shook the floorboards: the ogre entered, smelling fresh meat. Poking around the room with his iron-tipped club, he pulled the seven trembling boys from beneath the bed.

'Aha, wife!' roared the ogre, licking his lips. 'Here is a delicate roast for tomorrow's feast with my friends!'

The clever wife persuaded him to spare them until morning, as they had already eaten a fat sheep. The ogre ordered them put to bed in the chamber of his seven little daughters, who slept in a row wearing golden crowns upon their heads.

Thumbling noticed that the ogre was fond of tasting his food at midnight when he was in his cups. Taking the golden crowns from the sleeping daughters, he placed them on his brothers' heads and his own, and put their coarse wool nightcaps upon the ogre's daughters.

Sure enough, at midnight, the ogre stumbled into the dark bedchamber with his carving knife. Feeling the wool caps, he muttered: 'Aha! Here are the little rascals!' and in his drunken stupor, he dealt with his own daughters before stumbling back to bed.

The moment the ogre's snores shook the castle walls, Thumbling woke his brothers and they slipped through the garden wall into the forest.

At dawn, discovering his terrible error, the ogre roared with fury: 'Bring me my Seven-League Boots!' Putting on the magical boots, which expanded or contracted to fit any foot and allowed the wearer to cross seven leagues at a single stride, the ogre chased the boys like a hurricane.

Thumbling saw the giant bounding over mountains. He pushed his brothers into a hollow limestone cave beneath a high rock. Exhausted by his pursuit, the ogre lay down upon that very rock to rest and fell into a thunderous sleep.

Thumbling crept out, gently slipped the Seven-League Boots from the ogre's feet, and pulled them onto his own paws. The magical boots shrank to fit his little feet perfectly!

Leaving his brothers safely hidden, Thumbling sprinted in his magical boots straight to the ogre's castle. 'Madam,' he said to the weeping ogress, 'your husband has been captured by mountain bandits who swear to kill him unless you send all his gold and jewels! He commanded me to wear his Seven-League Boots as a token that you should deliver the ransom to me without delay!'

Terrified for her husband's life, the woman loaded Thumbling with sacks of emeralds, diamonds, and gold. Thumbling ran back, collected his six brothers, and led them home in triumph to their astonished parents.

With their boundless treasure, the family lived in great comfort and honor. Thumbling later served as the King's chief courier, using his Seven-League Boots to carry urgent dispatches across the realm, earning the love of the sovereign and the eternal gratitude of his brothers, proving forever that size is nothing compared to courage and wit.
moral: The smallest and least esteemed child often possesses the sharpest mind and becomes the salvation of the entire family. [TA]
